newsitem.title: HUNGARY: NATO official says alliance won't slow for Lebed.
newsitem.headline: NATO official says alliance won't slow for Lebed.

text.p: A senior NATO military official said on Tuesday the alliance would not slow its expansion process despite comments by Russia's outspoken security chief Alexander Lebed that it should not be hasty.

"NATO will stick to its chartered course -- it's nothing new and nothing confrontational," said General Klaus Naumann, the chairman of NATO's military committee, who was visiting Budapest to discuss cooperation with Hungary.
Naumann met Lebed on Monday in Brussels during the Russian national security adviser's visit to NATO headquarters, his first ever trip to a Western country.
After the meeting, Lebed voiced grudging acceptance of NATO's plans to enlarge eastwards to take in some of Moscow's former satellites in eastern and central Europe.
He acknowledged NATO's right to expand but said the problem was one of timing. "The main thing is not to hurry, or you may trip up," Lebed said.
Naumann described his talks with Lebed as constructive.
"They were conducted in a very civilised and moderate tone," he said. But he reaffirmed the timetable set out by NATO's political leaders would not change.

"What NATO wants to do is to achieve, in a converging process, a partnership with Russia that takes Russia's security interests into account and at the same time continues the course which NATO adopted in 1994 when the decision was taken that doors should be open to democratic nations," he said.
NATO intends to invite countries to open entry talks next year, with Poland, Hungary and the Czech republic seen as the most likely candidates.
Naumann said a third round of discussions with 10 countries interested in joining NATO would be completed by the end of October and the findings presented to the NATO Council.

He said he would be preparing a report on the military alternatives regarding any possible extension of the mandate for IFOR, the NATO-led peace implementation force in Bosnia, which is due to run out on December 20.
"As the NATO Secretary General (Javier Solana) has said, the NATO nations are aware that Bosnia cannot be left on its own next year," he said.

"The military authorities will be tasked to study alternatives for potential political decisions. This will be authorised by the NATO Council in due time and then we can come back to the political authorities with our ideas," Naumann said.
